Q134888199.summary: In the apse a youthful Christ with a golden cross-nimbus stands in a paradise landscape, holding a tall cross in his raised right hand and, in his veiled left, an open book inscribed with his words from John's Gospel: 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' and 'I and the Father are one.' The archangels Michael and Gabriel flank him with ceremonial staffs. On the wall above, Christ sits enthroned as heavenly ruler between two archangels, while the seven trumpet-bearing angels of the Apocalypse stand on either side; the names of Saints Cosmas and Damian survive in the spandrels. The mosaic proclaims Christ's full divinity, whether as victorious cross-bearer or as judge of the world.
facts: The mosaic was taken down from the Ravenna church in 1844 and is now in the Bode-Museum, Berlin; the museum notes that it has changed profoundly since then, as Enrico Pari's watercolour of 1842/43 shows.
The Lamb of God originally appeared in an aureole at the crown of the apse arch, and a frieze of doves, symbols of the apostles, decorated the soffit.
Today it measures about 4.3 m high and 6.15 m wide (museum inv. 6642).
Q134888199.notes: Much of the present surface reflects 19th-century removal and restoration, so details should be treated with caution. The figures of Cosmas and Damian themselves are no longer present; only their name labels are visible in the photograph.
Q134888199.original_title: Apsismosaik aus der Kirche San Michele in Africisco zu Ravenna

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-116-chris.summary: The young psalmist stands on a hillock among four groups of the nations and gazes up at a half-figure of the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos holding a book, attended by four angels. On a hill between them stand Mercy, holding a bowl of fruit and grain, and Truth with a scroll: 'his merciful kindness is great toward us: and the truth of the Lord endureth for ever'. It is the upper drawing on folio 67v, illustrating the shortest psalm.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-116-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:monumental-tokali-raising-of-lazarus.summary: At the left of this frieze, Christ, haloed, stands before the tomb where Lazarus appears wrapped in his grave-clothes, with Martha and Mary bowing at his feet; to the right follows the Entry into Jerusalem, captioned BAIOPHOROS ('palm-bearing'). The two episodes, which in the Gospel of John lead directly into Holy Week, are placed side by side as in the liturgy of Lazarus Saturday and Palm Sunday.
facts: Tokalı Kilise ('Church of the Buckle'), the largest church at Göreme, comprises an Old Church of the 10th century, painted in strips of red and green, and a larger New Church of the late 10th or early 11th century whose walls are dominated by rich indigo blue made from lapis lazuli.
In the Byzantine liturgical year the Raising of Lazarus (Lazarus Saturday) is celebrated on the day before Palm Sunday, which is why the two scenes are often paired.

cur:monumental-tokali-raising-of-lazarus.notes: The photograph shows a detail of the wall; whether the scene belongs to the Old or the New Church is not stated in the source. Dates for both phases are debated (c. 910s–920s for the Old Church; mid-10th to early 11th century for the New).
